newsitem.title: JAPAN: Forex market edgy, but analysts rule out trade war.
newsitem.headline: Forex market edgy, but analysts rule out trade war.

text.p: Currency markets got a taste of trade friction fears this week, but analysts say chances of a full-blown U.S.-Japan trade war look slim.
"For the Clinton adminstration, there is more risk than reward in starting a trade war," said Kenneth Landon, a currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"At this point in the U.S. economic cycle, there is strong growth and people are not being put out of jobs (by Japanese exports)," Landon said. "So politically, there is little for the Clinton administration to gain from a trade war that could have a negative impact on U.S. financial markets."

Comments by U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky early this week caused concern that trade tempers in Washington were fraying, prompting the dollar to dip briefly despite most pundits' view that the greenback's underlying trend is up.
Barshefsky told Reuters on Monday that Japan was not fulfilling a 1995 automotive trade pact and said signs of a widening car trade gap were disturbing.
The comments were followed by rumours later in the week that U.S. carmakers want Washington to review Japanese trade barriers.

A regular review of the 1995 car deal is set for the autumn and the U.S. Trade Representative's Office has a deadline of the end of September to compile its annual report to Congress on what actions it plans for the coming year, including monitoring of trade barriers or possible special proceedings that could lead to sanctions.

On Thursday, however, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his support for a strong dollar, telling Reuters it helped contain inflation. The comments helped boost the dollar against the yen to a close of about 118.65 yen in New York.

The dollar has been rising in recent weeks, buoyed by signs of sagging economic growth in Japan, expectations Europe's single currency will be weak when it is launched in 1999, and forecasts of a continued U.S.-Japan interest rate gap that favours investment in U.S. assets.

Still, perceptions that officials in both Washington and Tokyo are comfortable with a range of 110-120 yen to the dollar combined with Japan's bulging trade surplus mean currency players will remain sensitive to official comments on trade.

"You're seeing a Japanese trade surplus that's increasing and an exchange rate that allows Japanese companies to export at sizable profits," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo. "What it means is the current account surplus as a share of GDP (gross domestic product) by year-end will be above 2.5 percent, and that's awfully difficult to argue away."
Behind the widening trade gap is both strong U.S. growth and weak Japanese demand for imports due to Tokyo's tight fiscal policy aimed at getting its massive debt under control.
Rubin on Thursday, however, appeared to give Tokyo some breathing space on the fiscal front while waiting to see whether a domestic demand-led recovery materialised.
"Are they going to get their economy going again based on domestic demand? I think it's too early to know that," he said.
Clearly, Washington trade officials are annoyed by the persistent U.S. gap in car trade, which accounts for about two-thirds of the total two-way trade imbalance.
But analysts said Barshefsky lacked the political clout to push the U.S. administration to adopt a hawkish trade stance given the downside risks to U.S. markets of such a policy.

"Barshefsky...doesn't hold the weight in the cabinet that Rubin does and I can't imagine Rubin going along with that kind of policy given that the U.S. economy is doing just fine," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan.

Meanwhile, some U.S. trade posts have yet to be filled and Washington has still not appointed an ambassador to Tokyo some eight months after the departure of the previous envoy, making the United States look unprepared to wage a big trade battle.
"We've seen concern all year that they were going to play with the yen but they're not going to do it, plain and simple. The risk is too great and the benefits are too illusive," Bevacqua said.
While a rerun of the 1995 trade battles over cars is quite unlikely, economists say U.S. patience with Japan's sluggish domestic demand could run out in coming months.

"All he (Rubin) has to do is make some comment that exchange rates are one factor that help adjust unsustainable international imbalances," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
He said Rubin is unlikely to make such remarks, however, until after the late-September meeting of Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers and central bankers in Hong Kong.
"They want to give Japan a little more time and there are other issues to discuss (such as Asian currency turmoil)," Feldman said.
